statement: Week five, day one of the course: this week is about storage engines, which the teacher calls his personal favorite topic.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This week is all about storage engines. This is my personal favorite.

statement: The teacher has a strong affinity for databases, distributed storage and query engines; database systems was his favorite subject in B-Tech/M-Tech even though he scored a C grade in it, and he still formed a deep understanding of it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I scored a C grade in database systems.

statement: Today's agenda: designing a distributed cache, plus ETL and tiered storages; almost all papers the teacher reads are connected to distributed storage.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the agenda for today is designing distributed cache and ETL and tiered storages.

statement: The distributed cache discussion is built on the teacher's deep dive into the Redis source code - not just the low-level code but how Redis made certain design decisions; the teacher also has a separate course on Redis internals that goes deeper into Redis specifics.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I deep dive into Redis source code.

statement: The important design decisions made while designing the cache affect not just this system but almost every system: they are reusable Lego blocks / patterns that can be observed and copied ("control C, control V") with some modifications here or there.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: those Lego blocks, those patterns that you can observe and just control C, control V.

statement: There are only a few limited ways to achieve something; once you identify a pattern you can apply it elsewhere. That is why the last four weeks covered a vast variety of systems while always talking about the patterns.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: there are only a few limited ways to achieve something.

statement: So far in the course CDC was only written as a box in designs; this session goes deeper into CDCs and into how tiered storages are built.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Up until now, we just wrote CDC. Now we'll go deeper and we'll understand how tiered storages are built.

statement: While at Amazon, the teacher built something on top of tiered storage, which gave him a deep understanding of what tiered storages are and what happens behind the scenes.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: While I was at Amazon, I used to build something on top of it.

statement: This time the order is different: ETL and tiered storage come first, only as an introduction to form the dots (like the Kafka essentials session), then the distributed cache; the practical application of ETL and tiered storage comes tomorrow or next week when designing Amazon's order system.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I'll start with ETL. I'll start with tiered storage. Then we talk about distributed cache.

statement: The Amazon order system will be taken as one very detailed example, which will give an idea of how data pipelines are built in general - they are all derived from one or two basic ideas.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We'll take one very detailed example and understand how order system work at Amazon,

statement: Flow for today: tiered storage (ETL/CDC), then questions, then the distributed cache low-level implementation, then a break, then the remaining (high-level) details.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We cover low-level implementation detail. Then we go on a break

statement: Starting point: a day-zero multi-user blogging application has a database and an API server; the database cannot be exposed directly to users, so the API server talks to the database and abstracts out its complexities.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We cannot directly expose database to the user. That's why what we have, we have API server.

statement: When a company launches it typically does not focus on analytics or metrics; it only adds things like DAU, MAU or Google Analytics once some people use it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: when a company launches, they typically don't focus on analytics, metrics and whatnot.

statement: To understand how people use the product, the company starts measuring metrics such as number of blogs published, how many users are active, and how many people leave a like in the first hour.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: hey, number of blogs published, how many users are active, how many people leave a like in

statement: In a day-zero architecture there is no data warehouse: a visualization tool such as Grafana, Metabase or Tableau connects directly to the production database and fires queries on it to show visualizations.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you just have a visualization tool like Grafana or a Metabase or Tableau, which is connecting to your system, to your database directly.

statement: Querying the production database directly from a dashboard tool works fine until about Series A, i.e. up to roughly 10,000-50,000 users.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Works very well for Series A, till company, till 10,000, 50,000 users, right?

statement: As the application grows, the business needs data backing for important decisions; the CEO wants detailed reporting on particular user behaviour and recruits an insights team / business analysts, who need data to analyze the business.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Which is where CEO recruits insights team or business analyst.

statement: Exposing the production database to business analysts is very risky, even with read-only access, because it holds critical information including personally identifiable information.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: They say, oh, I'll only give read-only access. But this has critical information, personally identifiable information.

statement: The production database may be a NoSQL database like MongoDB, chosen because it sounded cool or fancy or suited the use case well.
case_study: Blogging app's primary store is MongoDB in the example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this database might be a NoSQL database like MongoDB.

statement: Business analysts know SQL very well and write very complex SQL queries with ease.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: They are champs at SQL.

statement: Every data warehouse (Redshift, BigQuery) and every data lake format supports SQL queries because everyone in the analytics domain is familiar with SQL - the teacher calls this a hard truth, not an assumption.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Every single data warehouse, Redshift, BigQuery, pick any data lake format, it all supports SQL queries

statement: Giving SQL-oriented analysts direct access to MongoDB would leave them with no idea what to do.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if you give them direct access to MongoDB, they'll go nuts.

statement: So the company starts writing a pipeline that takes data out of MongoDB and puts it into MySQL (the only SQL database it knows, in early times when it does not yet care about proper data analysis); the next question is how data moves from MongoDB to MySQL.
case_study: Blogging app: MongoDB -> MySQL for analysts.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You start taking data out of MongoDB and put it into MySQL because that's the only SQL data that you know, right?

statement: The natural progression: the API server publishes an event to Kafka whenever a blog is published, a consumer reads it from Kafka and writes it into MySQL in a particular format. The teacher presents this and then questions whether relying on API-server events is the best way.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So from API server, whenever a blog is published, Kafka, from Kafka, you consume it and you put it into MySQL in a particular format.

statement: The analytics copy must have no data misses: data must be consistent with the source - not necessarily real time, but eventually - because the business makes decisions on it and analysts only have access to the copy, so incorrect data means decisions on wrong data.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: there cannot be any data misses between this. You have to ensure data consistency across this data. May not be real time, but eventually.

statement: Not everything that happens in the database or application has an event: blog published or user profile updated may, but minor changes like count++ on views do not, because events are specific and contextual to the application while the analytics need is raw data.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: not everything that is happening in your database or in your application has an event.

statement: Not every event carries all the data: a blog-published event may carry only the blog ID, so the consumer needs complex logic to go and fetch the detailed information, which puts unnecessary load on the database and makes things messier.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if I just say blog published, I may just pass in blog ID. It does not have all the data, right?

statement: Relying on events pushed to Kafka and consumed by business logic sounds like the obvious answer but is not; there has to be a better, much more seamless way.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This sounds like an obvious answer, but it is not. There has to be a better way, a much more seamless way.

statement: CDC stands for Change Data Capture: any change in data is captured by CDC.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So CDC stands for Change Data Capture. So any changes in data is captured by CDC.
flags: check: "Very weird day" - possibly a misheard word or name

statement: Airbyte and Debezium are CDC tools; the teacher highly recommends installing and setting one up locally, Airbyte being the easiest to set up.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: At least Airbyte is the easiest one to set up.

statement: Instead of relying on API-server events, CDC tools rely on the actual source of truth - the database itself.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: instead of relying on API server events, we rely on the actual source of truth, the database itself.

statement: A CDC tool typically (not a hard rule) lets you configure source databases, transformation logic and sink databases; it pulls data from the source and puts it into the sink in the format you want.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: change data capture typically lets you configure your source databases, your transformation logic, and your sink databases.

statement: Because CDC operates on the database itself, updates for which the application server has no event are still captured and pushed to the other database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Your application server does not have an event for it. Still that updates will be captured

statement: With CDC, data is not lost if the application server crashes while pushing an event, because the pipeline relies on the source of truth; the teacher calls this the highlight of CDC.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's okay if your application server while pushing the event crashed.

statement: It is a very common concept (not a hard rule; some plugins work other ways) that CDC works on databases and internally keeps track of how far it has read - up to which rows, which column was updated.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Internally, it keeps track up until these rows.

statement: One way CDC reads the source is iterating tables row by row.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It reads tables row by row. One way to do it.

statement: Another way CDC reads the source is via the commit log / bin log, i.e. the WAL file: every commit is appended to the WAL, and CDC literally reads that WAL file and pushes the changes to the other database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Change data capture literally reads that WAL file and pushes the changes to this other database.

statement: How CDC reads depends on the bindings a database offers: MongoDB might choose not to expose its commit log, so CDC iterates collections; Elasticsearch does not offer one, so CDC iterates; MySQL has bin log support and exposes the WAL, so CDC reads it directly.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: MongoDB might choose not to expose the commit log file. So then change data capture will rely on iterating collections.

statement: For the user it does not matter how the data is read: you configure a source database, a sink and a transformation on the tool, and data flows.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So for you, it does not matter how the data is read from the database.

statement: If the source database is down, data is not captured; once it is back up, the CDC tool resumes from that point - that is the job of these tools.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But once this DB is back up, it will resume from that point.

statement: Relying directly on the source of truth instead of the API server is what makes CDC invaluable; the teacher says everyone uses it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This what makes change data capture invaluable. Everyone uses it.

statement: The sink of a CDC tool does not have to be a database: it can be Kafka, SQS, Kinesis, local disk or a number of databases - whatever plugins Airbyte or Debezium support.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Sink can be Kafka, SQS, Kinesis, local disk, certain number of databases and whatnot.

statement: Airbyte and Debezium are both open source: run them locally and play around - see how to configure them, what format data arrives in, and how to transform and push it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Run it locally, both open source.

statement: CDC is a great way to build replication across databases with some basic transformation in between.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So CDC is a great way to have to build replication across databases with some basic transformation in between.

statement: For bigger transformations there is Spark and similar tools, to be covered with data engineering basics, mostly next week.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: For bigger things, there is Spark and all which we will cover when we talk about data engineering basics mostly next week.

statement: Many systems designed earlier in the course, where the API server pushes to Kafka and a consumer acts on it, could be done with CDC instead; that does not mean one is better than the other - start with whatever works for you.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: A lot of things can be changed through CDC, right? It does not mean one is better than the other.

statement: The bifurcation: when you are moving raw data, go for CDC; when you need application context (when a particular event happens on the API server), have the API server push it to Kafka.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Whenever you are playing with the raw data you typically refer, you typically go for CDC.

statement: Transactional DB in MySQL to a search service in Elasticsearch: either the Kafka way (API server sends an event, a consumer ingests it into Elasticsearch) or CDC reading from MySQL and putting into Elasticsearch with an optional transformation (you may have to write your own); CDC then maintains the sync between the two databases.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So this way the sync between the two database is maintained by the CDC.

statement: From MySQL to a data warehouse such as Redshift, CDC can copy the relational data over and takes care of it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: from MySQL, you want to move data to a data warehouse. Let's say Redshift.

statement: If the data warehouse were fed from API-server events instead of the database, every new table or use case would require remembering whether its Kafka event was added - very inefficient.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Oh my God, have I added event to Kafka or not?

statement: Operating on raw data, CDC can bulk fetch rows from the source and bulk ingest them (e.g. into Redshift); an application-context pipeline with one event per blog published, consumed one by one, is very slow.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Operating on raw data, it can do bulk fetch, bulk ingest in Redshift and what not.

statement: CDC can also move data from a data warehouse like Redshift into S3, even though S3 is not a database, via plugins that write data into S3 in a particular form; Redshift itself also offers plugins for this, but the example shows how handy CDC is in many places.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you still want to take data from a transactional, from a data warehouse and put it into S3.

statement: Explore Airbyte and Debezium: how they are configured and which plugins they support; search YouTube for Airbyte and Debezium examples to understand their use cases.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Search for Airbyte example. Search for Debezium example.

statement: CDC will be used heavily in the next designs (tomorrow and next week) covering data engineering architectures and multi-tiered storage; today is just a gentle introduction.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We will use this very heavily when we design next systems tomorrow and the next week

statement: Consulting for a couple of organizations, the teacher saw data sync done with Kafka and high infra cost; he suggested switching to CDC, which cut that particular infra cost by 80% with much more reliability.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It brought down their particular infra cost by that particular infra cost by 80 percent and with much more reliability, right?

statement: Asked whether CDC reads the Postgres WAL via a Postgres client or with instance-level access to the WAL directory: the most basic configuration is via the Postgres client (the database's own client); some plugins extract the WAL files and process them; it depends on the plugin.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But the most basic configuration that you will find is via Postgres client.
flags: check: speaker boundary - "does it with" may be the start of the teacher's answer "Postgres client"

statement: A CDC tool is just something that keeps track of what it is reading, where it is writing and what its checkpoint is; there is no hard and fast rule for how it does it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it's just a tool which just keeps track that this is what I'm reading, this is where I'm writing, this is what my checkpoint is.

statement: Reading via the database client is better than reading raw log files: if the bin log / commit log format changes tomorrow, the plugin does not need updating because the client handles decoding.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Doing it with client is better because if tomorrow they change the format of bin log or commit log

statement: CDC via the client does not put a lot of load on the database because it is just a sequential read.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it does not put a lot of load because it's just a sequential read.

statement: Configure CDC on a replica rather than the master: spin up a new replica and point CDC at it, which cuts the load on the master database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And you can also configure it on a replica. You don't have to configure it on master.

statement: The 80% saving in the consulting story was only for that subsystem's infra cost, not the organization's entire infra cost.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: No, only for this component. So not entire cost, not entire infra cost

statement: In that organization, API servers pushed every single update to Kafka; a bunch of consumer workers transformed each event and wrote it to the other database - one read and one write at a time, with a very simple transformation. They could have batched but did not, "because that's how they thought systems are built".
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So they did not leverage batching at all.

statement: Because they did not batch, they needed more than 60 consumers - 60 machines with 32 GB each - just to handle incoming traffic.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So their number of consumers were more than 60 consumers, like 60 32 gigs machine.

statement: The teacher recommended configuring a simple CDC in Airbyte with a simple transformation and ingesting directly into the other database (both databases had Airbyte plugins); the workload went from 60 machines plus Kafka to two simple EC2 instances.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: From 60 machines and a Kafka, it got brought down to just two simple EC2 instances.

statement: Moving to CDC did not cost performance - they gained it: replication lag became bare minimum because these Java-written tools are multi-threaded, fetch in parallel, and are heavily optimized for minor transformations; reading and checkpointing are fast.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: They gained performance. Because now the replication lag is bare minimum.

statement: The old Kafka pipeline was silently losing data: their databases were out of sync and they had no idea; when told, they planned a cron job to resync and said losing data was okay - with CDC they stopped losing data.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Their databases were out of sync and they had no idea.

statement: CDC prevents data loss because it keeps track of which rows, documents or entities have been captured and pushed - it does checkpointing for you in a sequential way.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: CDC keeps track of which rows or which documents or which entities are captured and put there, right?

statement: A student suggested batching events would have solved the problem; the teacher agreed it would not have been as bad - they processed one at a time because it was the most basic thing to write, and it was a legacy architecture never changed as the company scaled.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: It would not have been as worse as it was.

statement: There is always some service in a company that no one ever touches; this legacy pipeline was one of them.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And you know, there is always a service. No one touches that ever.

statement: Running CDC from a read replica works just fine.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's fine. Works just fine.
flags: check: speaker of answer marked Teacher?

statement: CDC itself is eventually consistent - it does not guarantee strong consistency between source and sink databases - so using it with an eventually consistent NoSQL database is not a bad use case.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: even CDCs are eventually consistent. It does not guarantee strong consistency anyway.

statement: Where you need strong consistency you need synchronous processing; so CDC (asynchronous) cannot be used where synchronous communication is required - a student's restatement the teacher agreed with.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: When you need strong consistency, that's when you do synchronous programming.

statement: CDC is not like server-sent events: SSE is front-end JavaScript where the backend server sends events to the front end, while CDC is backend - it pulls data from a database, transforms it and pushes it to another database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Server sent event is front end JavaScript.

statement: Asked why the organization did not use SQS instead of expensive Kafka: a company always has decisions made a certain way; at their throughput Kafka's and SQS's cost would have been fairly similar. The service started basic, the company grew, it was never refactored, and it started to bite back.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It started as a very basic service. Company grew. They did not refactor that service. And then it started to bite back.

statement: CDC is a brilliant fit for capturing transactions in order: a transaction is an atomic unit, and when it commits, all of its statements (e.g. 10 SQL statements) are written to the log file in one shot, which CDC then reads.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: CDC is a brilliant use case for that.

statement: The sequence in which transactions commit and are added to the log file is the same sequence in which CDC reads them and pushes them into the other database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So the sequence in which your transactions are committing and added to the log file is the same sequence in which CDC is reading

statement: For complex transformations - multiple joins across tables, multiple aggregations, multiple jobs - CDC is not the tool; Apache Spark solves that.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Apache Spark solves that for you.

statement: Apache Spark is the king of the big data tools at the moment and is your friend for complex transformations across tables and joins.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Apache Spark is the king of all at the moment.

statement: CDC is for simple use cases: consume whatever is written in the source, extract it, and put it somewhere, with basic transformation.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You just want to consume whatever is written there, extract it out, put it somewhere, right.

statement: PG sync, a tool a student had used to push Postgres data into Elasticsearch, is an example of a Postgres-based CDC - it only works with Postgres but does exactly what a CDC does.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: PG sync is an example of Postgres based CDC because it only works with Postgres

statement: PG sync could be replaced with Airbyte or Debezium, which have much fancier plugins, so pushing data into some other system does not require rewriting integrations.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So now you could replace that with Airbyte, Debezium, having much more, having much more fancier plugins.

statement: The distributed cache is the teacher's personal favorite discussion: lots of brainstorming and critical questions, going into the nitty-gritty, granular details that matter.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the big discussion, my personal favorite distributed cache, will have a ton of brainstorming.

statement: Requirements of the distributed cache: high throughput, low latency, distributed - "everything we want, we are very greedy" - with scale given by default.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: High throughput, low latency, distributed. Everything we want. We are very greedy.

statement: The cache implements four functionalities: get, put, delete and TTL.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the four functionalities that would implement.

statement: The design has two brainstorms: first the low-level implementation, then (after the break) the high-level implementation covering consistent hashing and distributed hash tables.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Then we do high-level implementation of it, where I would want to talk about consistent hashing, distributed hash tables, those part.

statement: The system being designed is explicitly a distributed in-memory cache.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it is a distributed in-memory cache.

statement: The low-level brainstorm covers: storage, how to find that the cache is full, cache eviction, communication, concurrency and TTL - the things that matter most when implementing a cache.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: storage, how do we find caches full, cache eviction, communication, concurrency and TTL.

statement: The first discussion is a single-node implementation of the distributed cache; distribution comes with the high-level details.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is just single node implementation of distributed cache

statement: A student proposed storing key-value pairs with a contiguous in-memory array for keys, each holding a pointer to where the value is stored; the teacher summed it up as a hash table.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: maybe we can provide a continuous array of in-memory, which provides the location for keys, which holds the pointer where the values will be stored

statement: Single-node storage of the cache, put simply, is a hash table (hash map) of keys to values.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: To put it simply, hash table.

statement: A student wanted to handle open addressing vs chaining for a fixed-size hash table in the cache.
detail: Teacher's correction: hash maps already exist and have solved that problem, so there is no reason to rebuild that logic.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: If hash maps already exist, why would you want to rebuild that logic?

statement: A student moved on to how storage works when more than one machine is connected.
detail: Teacher's correction: the discussion is still the single-node implementation; for distributing across machines, think of sharding.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: No, no, no. We're still talking about single node implementation. Distribute machine, you can think of sharding.

statement: Changed requirement: the value can be a set, list, bloom filter, HyperLogLog and more - multiple value types - so how should the value be represented?
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now imagine in the value we could store set, list, bloom filter and HyperLogLog and whatnot.

statement: A student's answer, as in Java: the value is a general object; store a pointer to the object, which lives in the heap, or store primitive values in place of pointers. The teacher praised the use of the term primitive values.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: if it is like a primitive values, as we said, we can store in place, in place of pointers.

statement: The cache must know each value's type because commands depend on it - a set supports add, a list supports push - so before executing a command it must check that the value is of the right type.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If it's a set, I need to support add command. If it's a list, I need to support push command.

statement: A student proposed storing type metadata with the key, since everything is accessed via the key. The teacher countered: the key is a string, and prefixing it or turning it into an object makes lookups complicated (dereferencing every time); better to keep the key a normal key and put the type in the value.
detail: Teacher first said "Perfect" to adding something to identify the type, then asked "But why key? Why not value?" and gave the lookup-complexity argument. The student later defended the key-side idea on space grounds (see K1-099).
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So we need to have definitely with the key some metadata, which talks about this key represents a data type

statement: Teacher's design: store the key as a normal key and make the value a custom type ("my value") with two fields - a value that is a void pointer / object type able to refer to anything, and a type integer where 0 = string, 1 = integer, 2 = set, 3 = list.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you store key as a normal key and in the value, you create your own custom type.
flags: asr: [?two is set | asr: "to a set"]

statement: Executing a typed command (e.g. add on key "my set"): get the value, read its type, check whether that type supports the operation; if yes, typecast the object and perform the operation.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You see if this, the type that you have supports this operation or not. If yes, you use this object and you then typecast it

statement: A student argued for a bit-level optimization: only about 5-10 data types are needed, so a few bits suffice - half a byte (4 bits) gives 16 types, a full byte gives 2^8 for the next 10-20 years - and a wrapper on the value costs more processing. The teacher called it a brilliant point.
detail: Student's intermediate arithmetic as spoken: "two bits ... four options. If I add three, I will get nine options".
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Maybe just representing half of a byte, four bits, will give me 16 different data types possible.

statement: Redis uses four bits to store the value type, because the number of data types can never go beyond a certain number - they cap it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Which is why Redis does this. It uses four bits to store it

statement: When designing something in memory, be very cautious about every single byte and bit you use and get the max out of it, because RAM is very costly; always reduce space to the bare minimum you can work with.
detail: Repeated at 00:41:58: "always think of saving every single bit of data, every single byte at your using. If not, reduce to the bare minimum".
speaker: teacher
verbatim: get the max out of it, because RAM is very costly.

statement: Redis stores a lot of other meta information alongside the type, which is why the value is wrapped in an object; in Redis it is a struct (Redis is built in C), which makes it extensible - the extra fields come up later with features like eviction.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: In Redis it's struct, it built in C.

statement: Objects allocated with malloc or new (whatever the language uses) are allocated in the program's heap memory.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: whenever we do malloc, wherever we are allocating the objects, new, malloc, whatever you are using, it allocates the object in this heap.

statement: Asked what happens when the program heap is exhausted, a student answered that the eviction policy runs.
detail: Teacher's correction: the cache runs an eviction policy, but the question is about the program heap itself (continuous malloc).
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: No, no, no. That cache runs eviction policy. But in the program heap that you have

statement: Thought experiment: malloc a 1 MB chunk in an infinite loop with 1 GB of RAM - after 1024 iterations everything is exhausted; what happens on iteration 1025?
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you have one GB RAM, after 1024 iterations, you're exhausting everything.

statement: A student guessed that on heap exhaustion the system moves data from memory to disk to make space.
detail: Teacher's correction: when you try to allocate beyond the maximum limit the operating system gives a segmentation fault and the program crashes.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: I guess to allocate some space, it moves the data from a memory to a disk.

statement: Allocating beyond your allocated heap causes a segmentation fault: you are entering someone else's territory and your program crashes.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Segmentation fault. Right? Your program crashes.

statement: Coding in C in the first and second year of engineering, everyone suffered segmentation faults from trying to access memory allocated by someone else.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we tried to access memory allocated by someone.

statement: Crashing is one of the main reasons you never want to go beyond the heap / memory assigned to you.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this is one of the main reasons why you don't want to go beyond the heap that you have

statement: The cache must keep running no matter what and never crash, which means it has to cap its memory usage; the first question is how to find how much memory the cache is using.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It should not crash anytime, which means we have to cap the memory usage.
flags: check: sentence starts mid-way; words may be missing before "responsibility"

statement: A student suggested using a command to find how much memory the cache process uses.
detail: Teacher's correction: such a command 100% exists but is very expensive and not performant enough - every call becomes a system call, because the amount of memory a process consumes is known by the kernel.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So command is not a way to do it. Not denying it, but not performant enough.

statement: A system call causes an OS interrupt, and doing it on every memory check would slow down the entire system.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: System call causes an interrupt. It would slow down your entire system.

statement: Instead of an OS command, the cache writes its own size function.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Let's write our own size function.

statement: A student proposed computing size from the number of keys stored and the size of each key-value pair; the teacher refined it to maintaining a running counter: size += n every time a key or value is added.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Instead of that, let's just do size is plus equal to n every time we are adding a key or a value.

statement: The challenge is how much to add: sizeof of the value structure is fixed ("four bytes") but the value pointer may point to something taking far more memory, so the size is not deterministic from the struct alone.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But in reality, this might be taking up a lot more than that.

statement: Every cache maintains its own size counter rather than using an OS command, because the command is very expensive.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is exactly what every single cache does, because using command is very expensive.

statement: Hint toward the solution: look at how memory is allocated; the explanation uses C but holds for Java, Python or any language.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Assume you are writing code in C. It holds true for Java, Python, whichever language you are using.

statement: malloc allocates memory on the heap: you pass the size you want, malloc internally fires a system call, grabs memory in RAM and returns an address you can start using.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: In malloc we pass the size that we want to allocate

statement: free deallocates: it marks the location as free for the operating system, which can then allocate that same chunk to other processes.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Free basically marks that location as free for your operating system

statement: Adding a new key means creating the "my value" object: O = (my value *) malloc(sizeof(my value)) - allocate that many bytes and typecast; this object is what is stored in the hash table.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You will create object O is equal to my value star malloc. And then you pass size of bracket my value.

statement: A student proposed counting, on every allocation, size of my value plus four plus four for the pointer and type fields.
detail: Teacher's correction: sizeof(my value) already covers both fields, but the value pointer can point to, say, a 1 MB bloom filter - that is the interesting problem.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So size of my value plus four plus four.
flags: unclear: "the two point, the value point around the type pointer"
unclear: "This white pointer is for white, this is for white,"

statement: A student suggested the pointed-to data need not be specifically allocated on the heap.
detail: Teacher's correction: a stored bloom filter must also be allocated, through a malloc call; the student then agreed that its size must be added at that malloc call.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: We have to allocate that bloom filter, that let's say we are storing bloom filter in memory.

statement: Everything the cache stores (my value objects, bloom filters, sets, lists, linked list nodes) lives in the heap and is allocated through the same malloc (and released through free); so keep a counter updated on every malloc: size += size_alloc.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: anything we are ever allocating, we are invoking the same malloc function.

statement: A student proposed writing your own wrapper around malloc and free to keep the count; the teacher confirmed ("Exactly").
speaker: student (proposal)

statement: Redis wraps malloc in a function called zmalloc with the exact same signature: internally it does malloc of size B, adds B to total size (total_size += B), and returns the object.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So what Redis does, it just wrapped the malloc function under a function called zmalloc.

statement: With zmalloc, the global total-size variable always tells the memory the cache is consuming, without relying on an operating system command.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So now in the total size variable, which is global variable, you would always know the amount of memory that you are consuming.

statement: Redis still uses the OS command to check usage periodically / occasionally, which is fine, but in most cases the zmalloc counter is what is used.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Redis does that to periodically check on the usage, but it's still occasionally it's fine.

statement: Doing the size update in one wrapper is a simple, elegant solution to a tricky problem: the naive way of adding count updates at every malloc call site breaks if you forget even one of, say, 50,000 places.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So if you're doing malloc at 50,000 places, if one of the places you forgot to do total size plus equal to something, that's bad.

statement: In the Redis code base you never see malloc - you always see zmalloc, which has the same signature but updates the count internally.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: everywhere in the code base you would never see malloc. You would always see zmalloc

statement: When starting Redis or any in-memory cache you configure the total memory it may use, e.g. 1 GB - a user-defined soft limit, even though the machine might have 32 GB RAM.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Let's say you specify it as 1 GB. It's a soft limit.

statement: Enforcing the cap in zmalloc: before allocating, check whether total size + B exceeds the max limit; if so return an error, otherwise allocate and return the object.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if total size plus B is greater than max limit, you return an error.

statement: Alternatively zmalloc can trigger eviction: if total size + B goes beyond the limit, remove a key, then allocate, update total size and return the object - this is where the eviction algorithm plugs in.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If it is going beyond the limit, I can remove a key and then allocate

statement: Big systems are built on very simple solutions - nothing fancy; the zmalloc counter and cap check are basic logic that tells you exactly where to trigger eviction.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this is what tells you that how big systems are built on very simple solutions.

statement: The Redis source code is one of the easiest code bases to skim: after a few days (by the fifth or sixth day) you start understanding everything; the teacher thoroughly enjoyed reading it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Redis source code is one of the easiest source code that you can skim through.

statement: These design decisions help not just in designing a cache but many other systems: think in very simple solutions rather than going for something fancy or complex.
speaker: teacher
